opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's one of the best pieces of evidence we have for extrapolating toward the thing we actually care about. A lot of benchmarks measure something kind of narrow, like whether a model can answer multiple-choice questions or solve competition math problems, and they saturate quickly. Then you're left asking, "Okay, but what does that mean for when AI can actually do the job of an AI researcher?" It's hard to draw a line from those benchmarks to real-world transformative capability.

The METR horizon-length metric is different because it's measuring roughly the right kind of thing: how long a task, measured in how long it takes a skilled human, can an AI agent complete autonomously with some reliability, say 50 or 80 percent. And the real bottleneck for automating AI research, or a lot of knowledge work, isn't that models don't know enough facts. It's that they can't stay on track over long, messy, multistep projects. They get stuck, they don't notice their mistakes, they lose the thread. Horizon length is a pretty direct proxy for that agency and coherence.

And then the striking thing is how clean the trend has been. Over about six years, the horizon has been doubling roughly every seven months, and on more recent data it looks like it might be faster, closer to every four months. If you take that seriously and just extrapolate, you get from tasks that take humans an hour or two to tasks that take weeks or months within a few years. Once AIs can reliably do month-long projects, you're plausibly in territory where they can do a large fraction of what an AI research engineer does, and that's when you'd expect things to really accelerate, because AI starts speeding up AI progress itself.

Now, I want to be clear there are lots of caveats. The tasks are mostly software and research-engineering tasks, which are cleaner and more checkable than the real world. There's the question of what reliability threshold you need. There's uncertainty about whether the trend goes superexponential, which I actually think is somewhat likely, because at some point each doubling should get easier: going from a one-week to a two-week horizon probably requires less new skill than going from one minute to two minutes. Or it could slow down if we hit compute or data constraints. But as a quantitative anchor, it's the thing I'd point to first if someone asked, "Why do you think this might happen by the end of the decade?" It turned a lot of vibes-based argument into something you can actually plot on a graph and argue about.

r001.rationale: It projects tasks lasting weeks or months within a few years, but does not clearly specify month-long coding tasks at 80% reliability.

r002.rationale: It connects month-long projects to automating a large fraction of AI research, but does not clearly make that claim specifically for 80%-reliable month-long coding tasks.

r003.rationale: It notes uncertainty about whether the trend may speed up or slow down, but does not propose that timeline discussions should focus on assessing changes in its rate.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the reason I keep coming back to it is that it's one of the very few metrics we have that actually tracks the thing we care about, rather than some proxy that saturates and stops telling you anything.

Most benchmarks have this problem where a model goes from 20 percent to 90 percent and then everyone shrugs and moves on to the next benchmark. You can't draw a trend line through a saturated test. What METR did was pick a quantity that doesn't have a ceiling in the same way: how long a task, measured in human expert time, can the system complete reliably? A model that can do fifteen-minute tasks, then one that can do hour-long tasks, then day-long tasks. That axis just keeps going, and the horizon is the whole point.

And when they measured it, the striking thing was that it looked like a fairly clean exponential. The doubling time came out around seven months over a span of several years, and if you look only at the more recent models it looks more like four months or so. That's remarkable on its own, but what makes it important for timelines is that you can ask a concrete question: what happens when you extrapolate? If the horizon is at a few hours now and doubles every four to seven months, you hit tasks that take a human a full work week within a couple of years, and tasks that take a month not long after that.

That matters because I think the core bottleneck for AI systems actually automating research, including AI research itself, isn't raw intelligence in some narrow sense. It's the ability to pursue a long, messy, multi-step goal without falling apart. Being able to hold a plan together, notice when something's gone wrong, recover, and keep going. Task horizon is a pretty direct measurement of exactly that capability. So when I'm thinking about when we might get something like an automated AI researcher, that trend is a big part of how I get my dates.

Now, I want to be careful. It's a noisy measurement, the task suite is weighted toward software and research-style problems, and reliably completing a task in a clean benchmark environment is not the same as doing it inside a real organization with all the context and politics and ambiguity that implies. There's a real question of how much to discount for that gap. And exponentials don't go forever; this one could bend. But the honest thing to say is that so far it hasn't bent, and if anything it's been bending the wrong way for people who want to feel relaxed. When I update my timelines, that chart is one of the first things I look at.

r001.rationale: The response says a month-long task horizon may arrive “not long” after reaching a full work week, but it does not specify 80% reliability or identify these as month-long coding tasks.

r002.rationale: It connects the trend to timelines for an automated AI researcher, but does not say that month-long coding ability at 80% reliability would mean AI is approaching automation of large portions of AI research.

r003.rationale: The response notes that the trend could bend and says it has not bent so far, but does not propose that timeline discussions focus on assessing changes in the trend’s rate of progress.

astra-6.text:
Because it gets at a question that matters much more than whether an AI can answer a difficult exam question: how long can it carry out useful work before it gets stuck or makes a mistake that derails the task?

The task length here is measured by how long the task takes a human, rather than how long the AI runs. So you can imagine progressing from tasks that take a human a few minutes, to tasks that take hours, to tasks that take days. If you see a reasonably consistent trend in that quantity, you have something you can extrapolate, cautiously, toward systems that can carry out substantial projects autonomously.

For timelines, I’m particularly interested in when systems can do long, complicated AI research and engineering tasks. At that point, they could help accelerate the process of building better AI systems. So this measure potentially connects current capabilities to a mechanism for much faster progress.

Now, it’s not a countdown clock. A task that takes a human a day in a well-specified testing environment isn’t necessarily representative of a day of work in a real organisation. There are issues around how tasks are selected, what reliability you require, and whether the trend continues. But it’s a much more concrete piece of evidence than simply saying that models seem to be getting smarter. It gives us a way to make forecasts and then check whether capabilities are advancing as expected.

r001.rationale: The response discusses cautiously extrapolating task duration, but does not state that this implies roughly month-long coding tasks at 80% reliability.

r002.rationale: It connects long AI research and engineering tasks with accelerating AI progress, but does not say that systems capable of month-long coding tasks at 80% reliability may be nearing the ability to automate large portions of AI research.

r003.rationale: The response says to extrapolate the trend cautiously and notes that it may not continue, but does not propose focusing on how the trend’s rate of progress might change.

sol-6.1.text:
The reason I find it so important is that it gets at something much closer to what we actually care about than a typical benchmark score. It’s one thing for an AI to answer a difficult question. It’s another for it to carry out a project that would take a human hours or days, keeping track of what it’s doing, noticing mistakes, and recovering from them.

METR measures task length in terms of how long the task takes a human, rather than how long the AI spends on it. And the striking finding is that the length of tasks these systems can complete at a given level of reliability has been increasing roughly exponentially, with a doubling time of around seven months.

If that trend continues, you go from systems that can do short tasks to systems that can carry out substantial projects over a surprisingly small number of years. That matters enormously for timelines, especially when the projects involve AI research itself. A system that can autonomously do useful research could help accelerate the development of its successors.

Now, I wouldn’t treat that as a law of nature. The tasks are concentrated in particular domains, and doing a bounded software task isn’t the same as doing someone’s entire job. But it gives us a quantitative trend that bears directly on autonomous capability. It makes the possibility of very powerful systems arriving soon much harder to dismiss.

r001.rationale: The response reports a roughly seven-month doubling time and projects substantial projects, but does not state that a couple of years could yield roughly month-long coding tasks at 80% reliability.

r002.rationale: It connects autonomous AI research to accelerating successor development, but does not link month-long coding tasks at 80% reliability to approaching automation of large portions of AI research.

r003.rationale: It says the trend matters for timelines, but does not propose focusing timeline discussions on assessing how the trend’s rate of progress might change.
